nodes.title: Euclid's proof
nodes.text: A finite set $\{p_1, \dots, p_r\}$ cannot be the collection of \emph{all} prime numbers.

nodes.title: Second Proof
nodes.text: Any two Fermat numbers $F_n := 2^{2^n} + 1$ are relatively prime.

nodes.title: Third Proof
nodes.text: There is no largest prime.

nodes.title: Fourth Proof
nodes.text: The prime counting function is unbounded

nodes.title: Fifth Proof
nodes.text: The set of primes \(\mathbb{P}\) is infinite.

nodes.title: Sixth Proof
nodes.text: The series \(\sum_{p\in\mathbb{P}}\frac 1 p\) diverges.
If the sequence \(S = (s_1, s_2, s_3, \dots)\) is almost injective and of subexponential growth, then the set \(\mathbb{P}_S\) of primes that divide some member of $S$ is infinite.

nodes.title: Infinity of primes
nodes.text: There are infinitely many primes. (Six + infinitely many proofs)

nodes.title: Bertrand's postulate
nodes.text: For any positive natural number, there is a prime which is greater than it, but no more than twice as large.
For all \(n \in \mathbb{N}\) \[ \log n + \frac 1 n < H_n < \log n + 1. \]
For all \(n \in \mathbb{N}\) \[ e\left(\frac{n}{e}\right)^n < n! < en\left(\frac{n}{e}\right)^n. \]
\[\binom{n}{k} \le \frac{n^k}{k!} \le \frac{n^k}{2^{k - 1}}\]

nodes.title: Sylvester's theorem
nodes.text: For all positive natural \(n, k\) such that \(n \ge 2k\), at least one of the numbers \(n, n - 1, \dots, n - k + 1\) has a prime divisor $p$ greater than $k$, or, equivalently the binomial coefficient \(\binom{n}{k}\) always has a prime factor \(p > k\).

nodes.title: Binomial coefficients are (almost) never powers
nodes.text: The equation \(\binom n k = m ^ l\) has no integer solutions with \(l \ge 2\) and \(4 \le k \le n - 4\).

nodes.title: Lemma 1
nodes.text: For primes \(p = 4m + 1\) the equation \(s^2 \equiv -1 (\mod p)\) has two solutions \(s \in \{1, 2, \dots, p - 1\}\), for \(p = 2\) there is one such solution, while for primes of the form \(p = 4m + 3\) there is no solution.

nodes.title: Lemma 2
nodes.text: No number \(n = 4m + 3\) is a sum of two squares.

nodes.title: First proof
nodes.text: Every prime of the form \(p = 4m + 1\) is a sum of two squares, that is, it can be written as \(p = x^2 + y^2\) for some natural numbers \(x,y \in \mathbb{N}\).

nodes.title: Second proof
nodes.text: Every prime of the form \(p = 4m + 1\) is a sum of two squares, that is, it can be written as \(p = x^2 + y^2\) for some natural numbers \(x,y \in \mathbb{N}\).

nodes.title: Third proof
nodes.text: Every prime of the form \(p = 4m + 1\) is a sum of two squares, that is, it can be written as \(p = x^2 + y^2\) for some natural numbers \(x,y \in \mathbb{N}\).
A natural number \(n\) can be represented as a sum of two squares if and only if every prime factor of the form \(p = 4m + 3\) appears with an even exponent in the prime decomposition of \(n\).

nodes.title: Fermat's little theorem
nodes.text: For \(a \not\equiv 0 \pmod{p}\), \[ a^{p - 1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p} \]

nodes.title: Euler's criterion
nodes.text: For \(a \not\equiv 0 \pmod{p}\), \[ (\frac{a}{p}) \equiv a ^{\frac{p-1}{2}} \pmod{p} \]

nodes.title: Product Rule
nodes.text: \begin{equation} (\frac{ab}{p}) = (\frac{a}{p}) \cdot (\frac{b}{p}) \end{equation}

nodes.title: Lemma of Gauss
nodes.text: Suppose $a \not\equiv 0 \pmod{p}$. Take the numbers $1a, 2a, \dots, \frac{p-1}{2}a$ and reduce them modulo $p$ to the residue system smallest in absolute value, $ia \equiv r_i \pmod{p}$ with $-\frac{p-1}{2} \le r_i \le \frac{p-1}{2}$ for all $i$. Then \[ (\frac{a}{p}) = (-1)^s, \quad \text{where } s = \#\{i : r_i < 0\}. \]

nodes.title: Quadratic reciprocity I
nodes.text: Let $p$ and $q$ be different odd primes. Then \[ (\frac{q}{p})(\frac{p}{q}) = (-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2} \frac{q-1}{2}}. \]
The multiplicative group of a finite field is cyclic.

nodes.title: A
nodes.text: Let $p$ and $q$ be distinct odd primes, and consider the finite field $F$ with $q^{p-1}$ elements. Then for any $a, b \in F$, $(a + b)^q = a^q + b^q$.

nodes.title: B
nodes.text: For the field $F$ defined in (A), there exists an element $\zeta \in F$ of multiplicative order $p$, that is, $\zeta^p = 1$. Moreover, we have a polynomial decomposition \[ x^p - 1 = (x - \zeta) (x - \zeta^2) \cdots (x - \zeta^p). \]

nodes.title: Quadratic reciprocity II
nodes.text: Let $p$ and $q$ be different odd primes. Then \[ (\frac{q}{p})(\frac{p}{q}) = (-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2} \frac{q-1}{2}}. \]

nodes.title: Roots of unity
nodes.text: The $n$-th roots of unity are \[ \lambda_k = e^{\frac{2k\pi i}{n}} = \cos(2k\pi/n) + i \sin(2k\pi/n), \quad 0 \le k \le n - 1. \]

nodes.title: Wedderburn's theorem
nodes.text: Every finite division ring is commutative.
If $A$ is a real symmetric $n \times n$ matrix that is not diagonal, that is, $\Od(A) > 0$, then there exists $U \in O(n)$ such that $\Od(U^T A U) < \Od(A)$.
For every real symmetric matrix $A$ there is a real orthogonal matrix $Q$ such that $Q^{T}AQ$ is diagonal.

nodes.title: Hadamard's inequality
nodes.text: For any real $n \times n$ matrix $A = (a_{ij})$ with $|a_{ij}| \le 1$, \[ |\det A| \le n^{n/2}. \]
If a Hadamard matrix of size $n \times n$ exists for $n > 2$, then $n$ must be a multiple of $4$.
Hadamard matrices exist for all $n = 2^m$.
There exists an $n \times n$ matrix with entries $\pm 1$ whose determinant is greater than $\sqrt{n!}$.
$e$ is irrational.
$e^2$ is irrational.

nodes.title: Little Lemma
nodes.text: For any $n \ge 1$ the integer $n!$ contains the prime factor $2$ at most $n-1$ times --- with equality if (and only if) $n$ is a power of two, $n = 2^m$.
$e^4$ is irrational.

\upshape For some fixed $n \ge 1$, let \[ f(x) = \frac{x^n (1-x)^n}{n!}. \] \begin{enumerate} \item[(i)] \itshape The function $f(x)$ is a polynomial of the form $f(x) = \frac{1}{n!} \sum_{i=n}^{2n} c_i x^i$, where the coefficients $c_i$ are integers. \end{enumerate}
\begin{enumerate} \item[(ii)] For $0 < x < 1$ we have $0 < f(x) < \frac{1}{n!}$. \end{enumerate}
\begin{enumerate} \item[(iii)] The derivatives $f^{(k)}(0)$ and $f^{(k)}(1)$ are integers for all $k \ge 0$. \end{enumerate}
$e^r$ is irrational for every $r \in \mathbb{Q} \setminus \{0\}$.
$\pi^2$ is irrational.
For every odd integer \(n \ge 3\), the number \[ A(n) := \frac{1}{\pi} \arccos \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\right) \] is irrational.

nodes.title: Four proofs of Euler's series
nodes.text: Collecting the proofs from the chapter.

nodes.title: Pearl Lemma
nodes.text: If $P$ and $Q$ are equidecomposable, then one can place a positive number of pearls (that is, assign positive integers) to all the segments of the decompositions $P = P_1 \cup \cdots \cup P_n$ and $Q = Q_1 \cup \cdots \cup Q_n$ in such a way that each edge of a piece $P_k$ receives the same number of pearls as the corresponding edge of $Q_k$.

nodes.title: Cone Lemma
nodes.text: If a system of homogeneous linear equations with integer coefficients has a positive \emph{real} solution, then it also has a positive \emph{integer} solution.

nodes.text: TODO
In any configuration of \(n\) points in the plane, not all on a line, there is a line which contains exactly two of the points.
Let \(P\) be a set of \(n\ge 3\) points in the plane, not all on a line. Then the set \(\mathcal{L}\) of lines passing through at least two points contains at least \(n\) lines.

Let \(X\) be a set of \(n\ge 3\) elements, and let \(A_1, \dots, A_m\) be proper subsets of \(X\), such that every pair of elements of \(X\) is contained in precisely one set \(A_i\). Then \(m\ge n\) holds.
If \(K_n\) is decomposed into complete bipartite subgraphs \(H_1, \dots, H_m\), then \(m \ge n - 1\).
If \(n\ge 3\) points in the plane do not lie on one single line, then they determine at least \(n - 1\) different slopes, where equality is possible only if \(n\) is odd and \(n \ge 5\).

nodes.title: Euler's formula
nodes.text: If \(G\) is a connected plane graph with \(n\) vertices, \(e\) edges and \(f\) faces, then \[ n - e + f = 2. \]
Let \(G\) be any simple plane graph with \(n>2\) vertices. Then \(G\) has at most \(3*n - 6\) edges.
Let \(G\) be any simple plane graph with \(n>2\) vertices. Then \(G\) has a vertex of degree at most \(5\).

Let \(G\) be any simple plane graph with \(n>2\) vertices. If the edges of \(G\) are two-colored, then there is a vertex of \(G\) with at most two color-changes in the cyclic order of the edges around the vertex.

nodes.title: Sylvester-Gallai
nodes.text: Given any set of \(n \ge 3\) points in the plane, not all on one line, there is always a line that contains exactly two of the points.

nodes.title: Monochromatic lines
nodes.text: Given any finite configuration of ``black'' and ``white'' points in the plane, not all on one line, there is always a ``monochromatic'' line: a line that contains at least two points of one color and none of the other.
Every elementary triangle \(\Delta = \conv\{p_0, p_1, p_2\}\subset \mathbb{R}^2\) has area \(A(\Delta)=12\)

nodes.title: Pick's theorem
nodes.text: The area of any (not necessarily convex) polygon \(Q\subset\mathbb{R}^2\) with integral vertices is given by \[ A(Q) = n_{int} + \frac{1}{2}n_{bd} - 1 \] where \(n_{int}\) and \(n_{bd}\) are the numbers of integral points in the interior respectively on the boundary of \(Q\).

nodes.title: Cauchy's rigidity
nodes.text: If two \(3\)-dimensional convex polyhedra \(P\) and \(P'\) are combinatorially equivalent with corresponding pairs of adjacent congruent, then also the angels between corresponding pairs of adjacent facets are equal (and thus \(P\) is congruent to \(P'\)).
If a link consists of disjoint perfect circles that are pairwise not linked, then the link is trivial
The Borromean rings are nontrivial, and they are also not equivalent to Tait's link No.~18
The Borromean rings cannot be build from three perfect circles
For every \(d\ge 2\), there is a family of \(2^d\) pairwise touching \(d\)-simplices in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) together with a transversal line that hits the interior of every single on of them.
For all \(d \ge 1\), we have \(f(d)< 2^{d+1}\).

For every \(d\), one has the following chain of inequalities: \begin{align} 2^d &\leq_{\text{(1)}} \max \left\{ \#S \,|\, S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d, \angle(s_i, s_j, s_k) \leq \frac{\pi}{2} \text{ for every } \{s_i, s_j, s_k\} \subseteq S \right\} \\ &\leq_{\text{(2)}} \max \left\{ \#S \,|\, S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d \text{ such that for any two points } \{s_i, s_j\} \subseteq S, \right. \nonumber \\ &\qquad\qquad \left. \text{there is a strip } S(i, j) \text{ that contains } S, \text{ with } s_i \text{ and } s_j \text{ lying in the parallel boundary hyperplanes of } S(i, j) \right\} \\ &=_{\text{(3)}} \max \left\{ \#S \,|\, S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d \text{ such that the translates } P - s_i, s_i \in S, \text{ of the convex hull } P := \text{conv}(S) \right. \nonumber \\ &\qquad\qquad \left. \text{intersect in a common point, but they only touch} \right\} \\ &\leq_{\text{(4)}} \max \left\{ \#S \,|\, S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d \text{ such that the translates } Q + s_i \text{ of some d-dimensional convex polytope } Q \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d \text{ touch pairwise} \right\} \\ &=_{\text{(5)}} \max \left\{ \#S \,|\, S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d \text{ such that the translates } Q^* + s_i \text{ of some d-dimensional centrally symmetric convex polytope } Q^* \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d \text{ touch pairwise} \right\} \\ &\leq_{\text{(6)}} 2^d. \end{align}

For every \(d\ge 2\), there is a set \(S\subset\{0, 1\}^d\) of \(2\lfloor\frac{sqrt{6}}{9}(\frac{2}{\sqrt(3)})^d\rfloor\) points in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) (vertices of the unit \(d\)-cube) that determine only acute angels. In particular, in dimension \(d = 34\) there is a set of \(72 > 2*34 - 1\) points with only acute angels.

nodes.title: Borsuk's conjecture
nodes.text: Let $q = p^m$ be a prime power, $n := 4q - 2$, and $d := \binom{n}{2} = (2q - 1)(4q - 3)$. Then there is a set $S \subseteq \{+1, -1\}^d$ of $2^{n-2}$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$ such that every partition of $S$, whose parts have smaller diameter than $S$, has at least \[ \frac{2^{n-2}}{\sum_{i=0}^{q-2} \binom{n-1}{i}} \] parts. For $q = 9$ this implies that the Borsuk conjecture is false in dimension $d = 561$. Furthermore, $f(d) > (1.2)\sqrt{d}$ holds for all large enough $d$.
The set of \(\mathbb{Q}\) of rational numbers is countable.
The set \(\mathbb{R}\) of real numbers is \emph{not} countable
The set \(\mathbb{R}^2\) of all ordered pairs of real numbers (that is, the real plane) has the same size as \(\mathbb{R}\).
If each of two sets \(M\) and \(N\) can be mapped injectively into the other, then there is a bijection from \(M\) to \(N\), that is \(|M| = |N|\).

If \(c > \aleph_1\), then every family \(\{f_\alpha\}\) satisfying \((P_0)\) is countable. If, on the other hand, \(c = \aleph_1\), then there exists some family \(\{f_\alpha\}\) with property \(P_0\) which has size \(c\).

Let \(\mu\) be an ordinal number and denote by \(W_\mu\) the set of ordinal numbers smaller than \(\mu\). Then the following holds: \begin{enumerate} \item The elements of \(W_\mu\) are pairwise comparable. \item If we order \(W_\mu\) according to their magnitude, then \(W_\mu\) is well-ordered and has ordinal number \(\mu\). \end{enumerate}

Every set of ordinal numbers (ordered according to magnitude) is well-ordered.
For every cardinal number \(\mathfrak{m}\), there is a definite next larger cardinal number.
Let the infinite set \(M\) have cardinality \(\mathfrak{m}\), and let \(M\) be well ordered according to the initial ordinal number \(\omega_{\mathfrak{m}}\). Then \(M\) has no last element.

Suppose \(\{A_\alpha\}\) is a family of size \(\mathfrak{m}\) of countable sets \(A_\alpha\), where \(\mathfrak{m}\) is an infinite cardinal. Then the union \(\bigcup_\alpha A_\alpha\) has size at most \(\mathfrak{m}\).

Let $\langle a, b \rangle$ be an inner product on a real vector space $V$ (with the norm $|a|^2 := \langle a, a \rangle$). Then \[ \langle a, b \rangle^2 \leq |a|^2 |b|^2 \] holds for all vectors $a, b \in V$, with equality if and only if $a$ and $b$ are linearly dependent.

nodes.title: First proof
nodes.text: Let $a_1, \dots, a_n$ be positive real numbers, then \[ \frac{n}{\frac{1}{a_1}+\dots+\frac{1}{a_n}} \le \sqrt[n]{a_1a_2\dots a_n} \le \frac{a_1+\dots+ a_n}{n} \] with equality in both cases if and only if all $a_i$'s are equal.

nodes.title: Another Proof
nodes.text: Let $a_1, \dots, a_n$ be positive real numbers, then \[ \frac{n}{\frac{1}{a_1}+\dots+\frac{1}{a_n}} \le \sqrt[n]{a_1a_2\dots a_n} \le \frac{a_1+\dots+ a_n}{n} \] with equality in both cases if and only if all $a_i$'s are equal.

nodes.title: Still another Proof
nodes.text: Let $a_1, \dots, a_n$ be positive real numbers, then \[ \frac{n}{\frac{1}{a_1}+\dots+\frac{1}{a_n}} \le \sqrt[n]{a_1a_2\dots a_n} \le \frac{a_1+\dots+ a_n}{n} \] with equality in both cases if and only if all $a_i$'s are equal.

Suppose all roots of the polynomial $x^n + a_{n-1}x^{n-1} + \dots + a_0$ are real. Then the roots are contained in the interval with the endpoints \[ -\frac{a_{n-1}}{n}\pm\frac{n-1}{n}\sqrt{a_{n-1}^2 - \frac{2n}{n-1}a_{n-2}}. \]

Let $f(x)$ be a real polynomial of degree $n \ge 2$ with only real roots, such that $f(x)> 0$ for $ -1 < x < 1$ amd $f(-1) = f(1) = 0$. Then \[ \frac{2}{3}T \le A \le \frac{2}{3}R, \] and equality holds in both cases only for $n=2$.
Suppose $G$ is a graph on $n$ vertices without triangles. Then $G$ has at most $\frac{n^2}{4}$ edges, and equality holds only when $n$ is even and $G$ is the complete bipartite graph $K_{n/2, n/2}$.
Suppose $G$ is a graph on $n$ vertices without triangles. Then $G$ has at most $\frac{n^2}{4}$ edges, and equality holds only when $n$ is even and $G$ is the complete bipartite graph $K_{n/2, n/2}$.
Let $p(z) = \sum_{k=0}^n c_k z^k$ be a complex polynomial of degree $n\ge 1$. If $p(a)\ne0$, then every disk $D$ around $a$ contains an interior point $b$ with $|p(b)| < |p(a)|$
Every nonconstant polynomial with complex coefficients has at least one root in the field of complex numbers.

Every dissection of the unit square $S = [0, 1]^2$ into finitely many triangles contains an odd number of rainbow triangles, and thus at least one.

nodes.title: Monsky's theorem
nodes.text: It is not possible to dissect a square into an odd number of triangles of equal algebra area.
A proper subring $R\subset K$ is a valuation ring with respect to some valuation $v$ into some ordered group $G$ if and only if $K = R \cup R^{-1}$.
The field of real numbers $\mathbb{R}$ has a non-Archimedean valuation to an ordered abelian group \[v: \mathbb{R} \to \{0\} \cup G\] such that $v(\frac{1}{2}) > 1$.

Let $f(z)$ be a complex polynomial of degree at least 1 and leading coefficient 1. Set $C = \{ z \in \mathbb{C} : |f(z)| \leq 2 \}$ and let $\mathcal{R}$ be the orthogonal projection of $C$ onto the real axis. Then there are intervals $I_1, \dots, I_t$ on the real line which together cover $\mathcal{R}$ and satisfy \[ \ell(I_1) + \cdots + \ell(I_t) \leq 4. \]

Let $p(x)$ be a real polynomial of degree $n \geq 1$ with leading coefficient 1, and all roots real. Then the set $\mathcal{P} = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : |p(x)| \leq 2\}$ can be covered by intervals of total length at most 4.
Let $p(x)$ be a real polynomial of degree $n \geq 1$ with leading coefficient 1, and suppose that $|p(x)| \leq 2$ for all $x$ in the interval $[a, b]$. Then $b - a \leq 4$.

nodes.title: Chebyshev's theorem
nodes.text: Let $p(x)$ be a real polynomial of degree $n \geq 1$ with leading coefficient 1. Then \[ \max_{-1 \leq x \leq 1} |p(x)| \geq \frac{1}{2^{n-1}}. \]

nodes.title: Fact 1
nodes.text: If $b$ is a multiple root of $p'(x)$, then $b$ is also a root of $p(x)$.

nodes.title: Fact 2
nodes.text: We have $p'(x)^2 \geq p(x)p''(x)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$.
Let $M = (m_{ij})$ be a doubly stochastic $n \times n$ matrix. Then \[\per M \ge \frac{n!}{n^n}\] and equality holds if and only if $m_{ij} = \frac{1}{n}$

nodes.title: Gurvit's proposition
nodes.text: If $p(x)\in \mathbb{R}_+[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ is a $H$-stable and homogeneous of degree $n$, then either $p'\cong 0$, or $p'$ is $H$-stable and homogeneous of degree $n - 1$. In either case \[ \mycap(p') \ge \mycap\cdot g(\deg_np). \]

Let $a_1, \dots, a_n$ be vectors in $\mathbb{R}^d$, each of length at least 1, and let $R_1, \dots, R_k$ be $k$ open regions of $\mathbb{R}^d$, where $|x - y| < 2$ for any $x, y$ that lie in the same region $R_i$. Then the number of linear combinations $\sum_{i=1}^{n} \epsilon_i a_i$, $\epsilon_i \in \{1, -1\}$, that can lie in the union $\bigcup_i R_i$ of the regions is at most the sum of the $k$ largest binomial coefficients $\binom{n}{j}$. In particular, we get the bound $\binom{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor}{n}$ for $k = 1$.

nodes.title: A
nodes.text: The functions $f$ and $g$ are defined for all non-integral values and are continuous there.

nodes.title: B
nodes.text: Both $f$ and $g$ are \emph{periodic} of period $1$, that is $f(x + 1) = f(x)$ and $g(x + 1) = g(x)$ hold for all $x\in \mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Z}$.

nodes.title: C
nodes.text: Both $f$ and $g$ are \emph{odd} functions, that is we have $f(-x) = -f(x)$ and $g(-x) = -g(x)$ for all $x\in \mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Z}$.

nodes.title: D
nodes.text: The two functions $f$ and $g$ satisfy the same functional equation: $f(\frac{x}{2}) + f(\frac{x + 1}{2}) = 2f(x)$ and $g(\frac{x}{2}) + g(\frac{x + 1}{2}) = gf(x)$.

nodes.title: E
nodes.text: By setting $h(x) := 0$ for $x \in \mathbb{Z}$, $h$ becomes a continuous function on all of $\mathbb{R}$ that shares the properties given in \ref{ch26lemma_b}, \ref{ch26lemma_c}, \ref{ch26lemma_d}.
\[ \pi\cot{\pi x} = \frac{1}{x} + \sum_{n = 1}^\infty \left(\frac{1}{x + n} + \frac{1}{x - n}\right) \] for $x\in \mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Z}$.

nodes.title: Buffon's needle problem
nodes.text: If a short needle, of length $\ell$, is dropped on paper that is ruled with equally spaced lines of distance $d \geq \ell$, then the probability that the needle comes to lie in a position where it crosses one of the lines is exactly \[ p = \frac{2 \ell}{\pi d}. \]

nodes.title: Pigeon-hole principle
nodes.text: If $n$ objects are placed in $r$ boxes, where $r < n$, then at least one of the boxes contains more than one object.

nodes.title: Claim
nodes.text: Consider the numbers $1, 2, 3, \dots, 2n$, and take any $n + 1$ of them. Then there are two among these $n + 1$ numbers which are relatively prime.

nodes.title: Claim
nodes.text: Suppose again $A \subset \{1, 2, \dots, 2n\}$ with $|A| = n+1$. Then there are always two numbers in $A$ such that one divides the other.

nodes.title: Claim (Erd\H{o}s--Szekeres)
nodes.text: In any sequence $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{mn+1}$ of $mn+1$ distinct real numbers, there exists an increasing subsequence \[ a_{i_1} < a_{i_2} < \cdots < a_{i_{m+1}} \quad (i_1 < i_2 < \cdots < i_{m+1}) \] of length $m+1$, or a decreasing subsequence \[ a_{j_1} > a_{j_2} > \cdots > a_{j_{n+1}} \quad (j_1 < j_2 < \cdots < j_{n+1}) \] of length $n+1$, or both.

nodes.title: Claim
nodes.text: Suppose we are given $n$ integers $a_1, \dots, a_n$, which need not be distinct. Then there is always a set of consecutive numbers $a_{k+1}, a_{k+2}, \dots, a_{\ell}$ whose sum $\sum_{i=k+1}^{\ell} a_i$ is a multiple of $n$.

nodes.title: Double counting
nodes.text: Suppose that we are given two finite sets $R$ and $C$ and a subset $S \subseteq R \times C$. Whenever $(p, q) \in S$, then we say $p$ and $q$ are incident. If $r_p$ denotes the number of elements that are incident to $p \in R$, and $c_q$ denotes the number of elements that are incident to $q \in C$, then \[ \sum_{p \in R} r_p = |S| = \sum_{q \in C} c_q. \tag{3} \]

nodes.title: Average number of divisors
nodes.text: For any positive integer $n$, \[ \sum_{j=1}^{n} t(j) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left\lfloor \frac{n}{i} \right\rfloor. \] Consequently, \[ \log n - 1 < \bar{t}(n) \leq H_n < \log n + 1, \] where $H_n = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{i}$ is the $n$-th harmonic number.

nodes.title: Handshaking
nodes.text: Let $G$ be a finite simple graph with vertex set $V$ and edge set $E$ and let $d(v)$ denote the degree of a vertex $v$. Then \[ \sum_{v\in V}d(v) = 2|E|. \tag{4} \]

nodes.title: Reiman
nodes.text: If the graph $G$ on $n$ vertices contains no $4$-cycles, then \[ |E| \leq \left\lfloor \frac{n}{4}\left(1 + \sqrt{4n - 3}\right) \right\rfloor. \tag{6} \]

nodes.title: Sperner's Lemma
nodes.text: Suppose that some ``big'' triangle with vertices $V_1, V_2, V_3$ is triangulated (that is, decomposed into a finite number of ``small'' triangles that fit together edge-by-edge). Assume that the vertices in the triangulation get ``colors'' from the set $\{1, 2, 3\}$ such that $V_i$ receives the color $i$ (for each $i$), and only the colors $i$ and $j$ are used for vertices along the edge from $V_i$ to $V_j$ (for $i \neq j$), while the interior vertices are colored arbitrarily with $1$, $2$, or $3$. Then in the triangulation there must be a small ``tricolored'' triangle, which has all three different vertex colors.

nodes.title: Hall's marriage theorem
nodes.text: Let $A_1, \dots A_n$ be a collection of subsets of a finite set $X$. Then there exists a system of distinct representatives if and only if the union of any $m$ sets $A_i$ contains at least $m$ elements, for $1 \le m \le n$.

nodes.title: $k$ systems of distinct representatives

Let $c \geq 0$ and $k := \lceil n \log n + cn \rceil$. Then after performing $k$ top-in-at-random shuffles on a deck of $n$ cards, the variation distance from the uniform distribution satisfies \[ d(k) := ||\text{Top}^*k - \mathbb{U}|| \leq e^{-c}. \]

After performing $k$ riffle shuffles on a deck of $n$ cards, the variation distance from a uniform distribution satisfies \[ ||\text{Rif}^*k - \mathbb{U}|| \leq 1 - \prod_{i=1}^{n-1} \left( 1 - \frac{i}{2^k} \right). \]

A matching $M$ of $G = (X \cup Y, E)$ is called \textit{stable} if the following condition holds: Whenever $uv \in E \setminus M$, $u \in X$, $v \in Y$, then either $uy \in M$ with $y > v$ in $N(u)$ or $xv \in M$ with $x > u$ in $N(v)$, or both.
